agent_explanations_oldest_first.text: Pass 12 for C(-1.5) is done, and the per-text means again changed only slightly. I'll compute the same table. If the onset logprob falls, and clearly more than the same-token novel-line control, this direction is a causal anti-repetition lever with the opposite sign to my original guess. If it doesn't, the onset-direction approach is closed.

This time the edit moves the decision in the predicted direction, and the dose response is consistent: β = +2 raised P(onset), and β = -1.5 lowers it.

| Measure (change vs original) | C(-1.5) |
|---|---|
| Onset first-token logprob, mean | -0.44 nats |
| Onset first-token logprob, median | -0.17 nats |
| P(onset) | 0.73 → 0.60 |
| Same-first-token novel lines | -0.12 nats (selectivity about 3.6:1) |
| In-loop copied tokens | -0.11 nats |
| Finished-answer tokens | -0.005 nats per token |
| Reference solutions | +0.011 nats per token |

So amplifying this "already said this" signal discourages starting and continuing repeats while leaving the reasoning text essentially untouched. That is the profile I wanted.

The real test is accuracy. I'll run a paired "both" generation on dev_b2, the last 256 DEV problems. They were not used to build the direction, since the onset texts came from dev_a and dev_b1. Two outcomes would confirm the mechanism: a clearly lower cut rate with accuracy at least as good (gain of about +2 or more), or many wrong→right flips among formerly cut answers. Unchanged cuts would refute it, as would cuts turning into wrong answers with a net loss.

dev_b2 holds 256 DEV problems with no overlap with HOLDOUT, and C(-1.5) is backed up. This paired generation measures the accuracy effect of amplifying the "already said" direction. I'm watching for fewer cuts at max tokens and a non-negative paired gain.

The loop repair works mechanically but doesn't improve accuracy:

| | Original | Edited C(-1.5) |
|---|---|---|
| Cut at max tokens | 29.7% | 15.6% |
| Mean tokens | 361 | 282 |
| Accuracy | 20.3% | 20.7% |

The paired gain is +0.4 ± 2.0 (13 wrong→right, 12 right→wrong). Most freed loops become wrong answers, which confirms the earlier finding that loops mostly occur on problems the model has already failed. By the stated criterion, accuracy not cut-offs, C alone is no improvement.

Before deciding how to use it, I'll inspect the paired items:
- accuracy of problems that were cut in the original but finished under C;
- whether C hurt problems that originally finished;
- how C behaves within each style (plain or markdown).

If formerly-cut problems that now finish are about as accurate as the original's finished answers on similar problems, C is neutral rather than harmful. Combining it with S could then let S's better plain-mode reasoning count without S's extra loops. If C damages already-finishing answers, the combination is unlikely to help.
